plan: Ten new items; topics checked against all verbal bank passages (a lichen central-idea item was replaced with Roman concrete because two lichen passages exist). inexhaustible/auspicious WIC, Roman concrete central idea, chess expertise inference, seed-dispersal two-part data, note-taking replication cross-text, Bessie Coleman synthesis (cause), 'Conversely,' transition, irregular plural possessive, past perfect progressive.

passages.title: A dependable spring
passages.text: The village's water supply had always seemed ______: even in the driest summers, the spring at the edge of town kept flowing as strongly as ever.

passages.title: Test wells
passages.text: The first season's results were ______: three of the four test wells drilled in the valley struck water, suggesting that the larger irrigation project could succeed.

passages.title: Concrete that mends itself
passages.text: Ancient Roman concrete often contains small white lumps of lime, which researchers long assumed were signs of careless mixing. A 2023 study suggested a different explanation. When cracks form and water seeps in, the lumps can dissolve and then harden again as a new mineral that fills the cracks. The lumps, in other words, may have helped some Roman structures repair their own damage over the centuries.

passages.title: Remembering the board
passages.text: In a classic study, chess experts and beginners were briefly shown chessboards and then asked to reconstruct them from memory. When the pieces were arranged as they might appear in a real game, the experts recalled far more of them than the beginners did. When the pieces were placed at random, however, the experts did only slightly better than the beginners. These results suggest that ______

passages.title: How far seeds travel
passages.text:
Researchers tracked how far two bird species carried the seeds of a fruiting tree before dropping them.
Bird species | Median distance (meters) | Longest distance recorded (meters)
Species A | 120 | 400
Species B | 60 | 900
The researchers concluded that species A usually carries seeds farther than species B does, but that species B occasionally carries seeds much farther than species A ever did.

passages.title: Notes by hand (two texts)
passages.text:
Text 1
In a widely cited 2014 study, students who took lecture notes by hand answered conceptual questions about the lecture better than students who typed notes on laptops. The researchers suggested that writing by hand, which is slower, forces students to summarize ideas rather than copy words, and so improves learning.
Text 2
Later researchers repeated the study's procedures with new groups of students. They found that differences between handwritten and typed notes were smaller and less consistent than originally reported, and in several comparisons there was no reliable difference at all.

passages.title: Training abroad
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Bessie Coleman wanted to become a pilot in the early 1920s.
• Flight schools in the United States refused to admit her because she was Black and a woman.
• She learned French and traveled to France to train.
• In 1921 she earned an international pilot's license there.
• She returned to the United States and performed in air shows.

passages.title: Water and storms
passages.text: Warm ocean water supplies the heat and moisture that power a hurricane, which is why storms often strengthen as they cross warm seas. ______ a hurricane that stalls over one area can churn up cooler water from below the surface, cutting off its own supply of warmth and weakening itself.

passages.title: Singing at the festival
passages.text: The ______ performance was the highlight of the town's spring festival, drawing a larger crowd than any of the professional acts.

passages.title: Building a dam
passages.text: Construction of Hoover Dam began in 1931. By the time the dam was completed in 1936, thousands of workers ______ on the project for about five years, often in extreme desert heat.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: kept flowing as strongly as ever
candidates.explanation: A spring that never weakens, even in drought, seems as if it could never run out: "inexhaustible."

A.rationale: Nothing in the text concerns the water's quality.

C.rationale: A spring that flows strongly even in the driest summers is not seasonal.

D.rationale: Cost is never mentioned; the point is that the water never ran out.

hints: Did the spring ever run low?
candidates.remember: Use the detail after the colon to define the blank.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: suggesting that the larger irrigation project could succeed
candidates.explanation: Results that point toward future success are a good sign: "auspicious."

A.rationale: Results that suggest success are not threatening.

B.rationale: Three successful wells out of four are not too small to matter.

C.rationale: The results point clearly toward success, so they are not unclear.

hints: Do the results point toward success or failure?
candidates.remember: A word describing early results often signals what they predict.

candidates.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Features once seen as flaws in Roman concrete may have helped it repair cracks.
choices.B: Roman builders mixed their concrete more carelessly than modern builders do.
choices.C: Modern concrete contains white lumps of lime that weaken its structure.
choices.D: Water seeping into cracks is the main cause of damage to ancient buildings.

candidates.evidence: may have helped some Roman structures repair their own damage
candidates.explanation: The text replaces an old view (the lumps were mistakes) with a new one (they helped seal cracks), which is its main point.

B.rationale: The text reports that this was a mistaken assumption about the lumps.

C.rationale: The text is about Roman concrete, and it suggests the lumps were useful.

D.rationale: Water is part of the repair process described, not presented as the main cause of damage.

hints: What was believed, and what does the new study suggest?

strategy.explanation: Summarize the shift the text describes.

candidates.remember: When a text overturns an assumption, the new view is usually the main idea.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: chess experts have better memories than beginners for any kind of information.
choices.B: beginners recall random boards more accurately than they recall real games.
choices.C: the experts' advantage came mainly from recognizing meaningful patterns.
choices.D: the study's random boards were too difficult for anyone to remember.

candidates.evidence: When the pieces were placed at random, however, the experts did only slightly better
candidates.explanation: The experts' large advantage appeared only when the positions made sense as real games and nearly vanished for random boards, so it came from recognizing familiar patterns rather than from a generally better memory.

A.rationale: If so, experts would have recalled random boards far better too.

B.rationale: The text compares experts with beginners, not beginners' scores across the two board types.

D.rationale: Both groups recalled some pieces; the point is the size of the experts' advantage.

hints: When did the experts' advantage nearly disappear?

strategy.explanation: Compare the two conditions before reading the choices.

candidates.remember: When an advantage shrinks under one condition, that condition reveals its source.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the researchers' conclusion?

choices.A: Species B's longest recorded distance, 900 meters, was the greatest of any value in the table.
choices.B: Species A's median was 120 meters to B's 60, but B's longest trip was 900 meters to A's 400.
choices.C: Species A's median distance was 120 meters, twice that of species B.
choices.D: Species A's longest recorded distance was more than three times its median distance.

candidates.evidence: species A usually carries seeds farther than species B does, but that species B occasionally
candidates.explanation: The conclusion has two parts: usual distance (the median: A 120 vs B 60) and occasional long trips (the longest: B 900 vs A 400). Only B supports both.

A.rationale: This supports only the second part of the conclusion.

C.rationale: This supports only the first part of the conclusion.

D.rationale: This compares two values for one species and addresses neither part of the conclusion.

hints: How many parts does the conclusion have?

strategy.explanation: Match each part of the claim to a column.

candidates.remember: A two-part claim needs evidence for both parts.

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would the researchers in Text 2 most likely respond to the suggestion in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing that typing notes on laptops reliably harms students' learning
choices.B: By arguing that typing notes produces much better learning than handwriting
choices.C: By claiming that the 2014 study's students were too few to draw any conclusions
choices.D: By arguing that the evidence for a handwriting advantage is weaker than Text 1 suggests

candidates.evidence: smaller and less consistent than originally reported
candidates.explanation: Text 2 repeated the study and found smaller, inconsistent or absent differences, so it would say the evidence for handwriting's advantage is weaker than Text 1 suggests, without claiming the reverse.

A.rationale: Text 2 found no reliable difference in several comparisons.

B.rationale: Text 2 does not report a typing advantage, only smaller or absent differences.

C.rationale: Text 2 reports its own results; it says nothing about the earlier sample size.

hints: Does Text 2 reverse Text 1's finding or weaken it?

strategy.explanation: Note how strong Text 2's claim is.

candidates.remember: A failed replication weakens a claim; it does not prove the opposite.

candidates.stem: The student wants to explain why Coleman trained in France. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Bessie Coleman earned an international pilot's license in France in the year 1921.
choices.B: After earning her license, Bessie Coleman returned to the United States to fly in air shows.
choices.C: Rejected by U.S. flight schools, Coleman learned French and trained in France instead.
choices.D: In the early 1920s, Bessie Coleman learned French because she wanted to become a pilot.

candidates.evidence: Flight schools in the United States refused to admit her
candidates.explanation: The reason she trained in France is that U.S. flight schools refused her; only C states that cause along with the result.

A.rationale: This states where she earned the license but not why she went there.

B.rationale: This describes what happened afterward, not why she trained abroad.

D.rationale: This omits the reason she needed to go abroad: U.S. schools refused her.

strategy.explanation: Find the choice that includes the cause.

candidates.remember: To explain why, include the cause, not just the event.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: cutting off its own supply of warmth and weakening itself
candidates.explanation: The first sentence explains how warm water strengthens storms; the second describes the reverse effect of cooler water, so "Conversely" fits.

B.rationale: Cooler water weakening a storm is the opposite of warm water strengthening it, not a similar point.

C.rationale: A storm weakening itself is not an example of storms strengthening over warm water.

D.rationale: Warm water strengthening storms does not cause a stalled storm to weaken.

hints: Is the second sentence the same idea or the reverse?
candidates.remember: "Conversely" introduces the reverse of the previous point.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: drawing a larger crowd than any of the professional acts
candidates.explanation: "Children" is an irregular plural, so its possessive is "children's"; the performance belongs to one choir, so "choir's."

A.rationale: "Children" is already plural, so it takes 's, not s'; and one choir performed.

B.rationale: One choir gave the performance, so the possessive "choir's" is needed.

C.rationale: "Childrens" is not a word; the plural of "child" is "children."

hints: Is "children" singular or plural, and how many choirs performed?

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: By the time the dam was completed in 1936
candidates.explanation: The work continued up to a past moment (1936), so the past perfect progressive "had been working" is correct.

A.rationale: The present perfect does not fit an action completed before a past event in 1936.

C.rationale: The present tense does not fit events in the 1930s.

D.rationale: The future perfect does not fit events that are already past.

hints: What tense does 'By the time ... was completed' call for?

strategy.explanation: Match the verb to a time before a past event.

candidates.remember: Use 'had been' + -ing for an action continuing up to a past moment.
